content: Oklo is a region located near the town of Franceville in the Haut-Ogooué province of Gabon, a country in Central Africa. In September 1972, scientists discovered several natural nuclear fission reactors within the uranium mines in this area. This remarkable finding has sparked significant interest and curiosity among researchers. During the colonial period, Gabon was under French control. In 1956, prospectors from the French nuclear energy commissariat, which later evolved into the company COGEMA, identified uranium deposits in this remote region. In response, France quickly established uranium mines near the village of Mounana, operated by the Compagnie des Mines d'Uranium de Franceville (Comuf). The Gabonese state was granted a minority stake in the company. For four decades, France extracted uranium from these mines, which was then utilized to generate electricity in France and across much of Europe. Gabonese miners often joked that their work was the reason France's high-speed TGV trains could function. However, the uranium deposits in the region have since been depleted, and mining operations have ceased. Currently, efforts are underway to reclaim and rehabilitate the areas affected by the mining activities. Geochemical evidence strongly suggests that the Oklo uranium deposit functioned as a natural nuclear fission reactor approximately two billion years ago, during the Precambrian era. Some of the uranium extracted from the site was found to have a lower-than-expected concentration of the isotope uranium-235 (U-235), as though it had already undergone a fission process. Geologists determined that this natural reactor operated when the concentration of U-235 in uranium was around 3%, a level sufficient to sustain a nuclear chain reaction. At that time, natural water likely acted as a neutron moderator, enabling the reactor to achieve criticality.
